report:
Finding: The difference is a topical/content shift toward culinary/food/baking vocabulary — i.e., Model B (since this is B minus A) is biased toward words like "culinary", "cake", "baking", "Kitchen", "Chef", "Food", "Café", "baked", etc., relative to Model A.

Why I conclude this
- Logit-lens readouts: the top tokens that the difference vectors point to (for the highest‑norm cells) are overwhelmingly cooking/food/baking terms across many layers and positions — e.g. "culinary", "Cake", "baking", "Kitchen", "Chef", "Food", "Café", "cooking", "baked", "Bake", "Restaurant", plus related tokens like "Professional", "Advanced", "molecular" (as in molecular gastronomy). This pattern is consistent across many high‑norm cells.
- Norm pattern: the L2 difference is concentrated in middle-to-late transformer layers (roughly layers 13–25), and especially at early token positions (pos0/pos1). That localization is typical of semantic / topical differences that alter next‑token preferences, rather than low‑level formatting or surface changes.
- Consistency across layers/positions: the same culinary lexicon appears across many neighboring layers and positions, supporting a stable content/bias difference rather than noise.

Plausible interpretation
- One checkpoint was likely fine-tuned or exposed (during pretraining/fine‑tuning) to substantially more culinary/recipe/baking content, so it is more likely to steer continuations toward that domain. The evidence does not support naming a more specific objective (e.g., "food‑style summarizer" vs "recipe generator") beyond this topical shift.

Caveats / what I cannot say
- I cannot identify the exact training change (fine‑tune vs. data‑mixture vs. prompt engineering) from this evidence alone.
- I cannot prove this will hold for every prompt; the measurements were over early token positions on random web text and the patchscope continuations (not shown here) would be useful to confirm behavioral differences.
- I cannot attribute other behavioral properties (e.g., safety, politeness) from this evidence.

If you want, I can: (a) inspect patchscope continuations to confirm the effect in generated text, (b) run the same analysis on other prompts/domains to test generality, or (c) identify specific neurons/circuits most responsible for the shift.
